section_summary: This section covers diplomatic despatches, State Department memoranda, intelligence reports, and telegrams from late April to early August 1936 documenting the political aftermath of the February 26 Incident in Japan. Key topics include the strategic debate over Japan's expansionism—specifically the Imperial Japanese Navy's 'southward advance' (Nanshin-ron) policy toward Southeast Asia versus the Army's continental advance—and the historic Diet speech by Minseito politician Takao Saito condemning military interference in government. The documents also record the secret court-martial trials and executions of rebel officers and Lt. Col. Saburo Aizawa, the eventual lifting of martial law in Tokyo, the policy initiatives of the Hirota Cabinet, and growing Japanese friction and wariness toward the United States as reported by military intelligence in Hawaii.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum evaluating Tokyo Despatch No. 1798 regarding the Japanese Navy's 'southward advance' doctrine.
subfiles.summary: Turner cautions Grew's 'southward advance' despatch overstates naval-faction talk and budget-parity seeking as approved government policy rather than hearsay.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1798 regarding Japan's Southward Advance Policy

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the Japanese Navy's 'oceanic' southward expansion doctrine versus the Army's continental expansionism.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew examines the revival of Japan's 'southward advance' policy championed by naval circles seeking raw materials, oil in the Netherlands East Indies, and trade expansion in the Pacific. He contrasts this 'oceanic' school with the Army's continental policy, noting that continental expansion has stalled due to risks of major war with the Soviet Union and Chinese resistance. The despatch details statements by Vice Admiral Takahashi, Foreign Minister Arita, Vice Minister Hasegawa, Netherlands Minister Pabst, and Shigeru Yoshida regarding Japanese ambitions and regional security implications.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1798: Japan's 'Southward Advance' Policy

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Despatch No. 1775 regarding political conditions and news censorship in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Despatch 1775 notes strict news censorship will hinder foreign missions from obtaining reliable Japanese political information.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 1775 on Political Conditions and News Censorship in Japan

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the abolition of the Cabinet Inquiry Council (Naikaku Shingi Kai) by Imperial Ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits the translated Imperial Ordinance abolishing the Cabinet Inquiry Council, countersigned by Hirota.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1816: Abolition of the Naikaku Shingi Kai (Cabinet Inquiry Council)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 1826 on Takao Saito's Diet speech denouncing military political meddling.
subfiles.summary: Turner summarizes Saito's Diet speech denouncing military political interference and censorship as causes of February 26, widely praised by press and public.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1826 regarding Takao Saito's Diet Speech

subfiles.about: Despatch and translated text of Minseito member Takao Saito's celebrated Diet speech condemning military political interference.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits and analyzes the speech delivered in the House of Representatives on May 7, 1936, by Takao Saito, accompanied by a full translation from the Japan Advertiser. Saito attacked the gullibility of young officers seduced by radical rightist ideologues like Shumei Okawa, condemned the assassinations of statesmen, and insisted on parliamentary governance and free speech. Grew reviews the responses of Premier Hirota and War Minister Terauchi, noting the extraordinary unanimous acclaim Saito received across Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1826: Speech Delivered in the Diet by Mr. Takao Saito on May 7

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum evaluating Tokyo Despatch No. 1833 on the aftermath of the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: Turner notes the Army's lost sympathy and Aizawa's death sentence, but warns the Hirota Cabinet's delayed reforms risk further violence while military grip tightens.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1833 regarding Aftermath of the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Despatch assessing the political dominance of the Army and the Hirota Cabinet's delay in reforms after the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the political climate following the February 26 Incident, highlighting public resentment toward militarism during Diet interpellations and the death sentence imposed on Lt. Col. Saburo Aizawa. Nevertheless, the military maintained martial law in Tokyo, secured larger appropriations, and established Three-Minister Conferences to influence foreign and domestic affairs. Meanwhile, the Hirota Cabinet introduced few concrete social or economic reforms, prompting public disappointment and warnings that administrative stagnation could provoke worse uprisings.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1833: Aftermath of the February 26th Incident

subfiles.about: Despatch on the Japanese Navy's pamphlet advocating oceanic expansion and the Australia-Japan Society's goodwill declaration.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports a Navy pamphlet pushing South Seas resource exploitation, countered by Australia-Japan Society resolutions denying territorial ambitions while reaffirming trade/raw-material needs.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1847: Japan's 'Southward Advance' Policy

subfiles.about: Letter from Fortune Magazine requesting permission to inspect Ambassador Grew's report on the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Fortune Magazine's Booth asks Dooman whether representatives may inspect Grew's February 26 report.
subfiles.title: Letter from Fortune Magazine Requesting Inspection of Ambassador Grew's Report on the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: State Department letter declining Fortune Magazine access to Ambassador Grew's report on the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Dooman regrets State cannot allow Fortune Magazine to inspect the confidential February 26 report.
subfiles.title: Letter from State Department Declining Fortune Magazine Access to Report on February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing rebel declarations transmitted from Peiping regarding the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: Turner reviews Peiping Despatch 472's translated Nonaka declarations denouncing the Genro and parties over the London Naval Treaty and Mazaki's removal, asserting Japan's messianic world mission.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Peiping Despatch No. 472 regarding Rebel Declarations in the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting the manifesto and declarations issued by Captain Shiro Nonaka and the February 26 rebel forces.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson forwards Harbin Despatch No. 227 by Consul General Walter A. Adams, which encloses translations and the original Japanese text of two declarations issued on February 26 and 28, 1936, by Captain Shiro Nonaka (mistranslated Noguchi) and the 'Righteous Army of Restoration.' The manifestos proclaim loyalty to the Emperor, denounce the Genro, party politicians, and corrupt cliques for undermining national defense and the imperial prerogative, and declare an armed uprising to achieve the Showa Restoration.
subfiles.title: Peiping Despatch No. 472: Declaration of Captain Shiro Noguchi and the Righteous Army of Restoration

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Despatch No. 1876 regarding passage of state security and mobilization secrets bills in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Despatch 1876 notes the Seditious Literature and Mobilization Secrets Bills faced resistance but passed in amended form.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 1876 on Seditious Literature Bill and Mobilization Secrets Bill

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting unconfirmed court-martial sentences against February 26 Incident participants.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports an unconfirmed death sentence for 19 officers in the February 26 trial, with over 40 others given five-to-fifteen-year prison terms.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 136: Unconfirmed Sentences in February 26 Incident Court Martial

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting War Office information on the progress of the February 26 trials and the continuation of martial law.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays War Office assurances to the attaché that verdicts come before July 10 with published findings, martial law continuing to prevent sympathy demonstrations, and Aizawa's appeal under review.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 140: War Office Statements on February 26 Trials and Martial Law

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum submitting Tokyo Despatch No. 1900 on Japan's political tensions to Secretary Hull.
subfiles.summary: Turner submits Despatch 1900 to Hull, summarizing internal rivalries, a strained civilian cabinet pressed by the military, and public unease over domestic crises.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Submitting Tokyo Despatch No. 1900 to Secretary Hull

subfiles.about: Despatch assessing factional tensions, the Army's six-year expansion plan, and preparations for ending martial law.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes internal political developments four months after the February 26 uprising, observing that while moderate Army leaders gained control, the military became even more dominant in national politics. The Army demanded a six-year, two-billion-yen defense program and threatened to withdraw support if political reforms stalled, while Navy Minister Nagano cautioned against naval involvement in politics. Political parties warned the government against further delay in reforms, and home and judicial authorities prepared security measures in anticipation of the repeal of martial law.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1900: Further Developments in the Situation Created by the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Brief telegram reporting the final rejection of Colonel Saburo Aizawa's death sentence appeal.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the supreme military court rejected Aizawa's appeal against his death sentence for Nagata's assassination.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 145: Rejection of Colonel Aizawa's Appeal

subfiles.about: Brief telegram reporting the execution of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Aizawa was executed by shooting on July 3, 1936.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 147: Execution of Colonel Aizawa

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing the official sentences pronounced in the February 26 Incident court martial.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports seventeen death sentences, five life terms, and prison terms up to fifteen years for February 26 insurgents, with officers convicted for unauthorized troop use and enlisted men cleared.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 149: Sentences Announced in February 26 Incident Court Martial

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the execution of fifteen leaders of the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports fifteen condemned participants were executed July 12, 1936, with public and press approving without disturbance.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 154: Executions of Thirteen Officers and Two Civilians for February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Brief telegram reporting the repeal of martial law in Tokyo by Imperial Ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Tokyo's martial law, in force since February 26, was formally repealed July 18, 1936.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 158: Repeal of Martial Law in Tokyo

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum transmitting a military intelligence report on hardening Japanese sentiment toward the United States.
subfiles.summary: FE submits an Army Hawaiian Department intelligence note that Honolulu's Japanese Consul General said the public is ready to fight the U.S. if necessary.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Transmitting Military Intelligence Report on Japanese Attitudes

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report quoting Japanese Consul General Tamura on rising nationalist bellicosity toward the United States.
subfiles.summary: Patton forwards Consul Tamura's interview expressing indignation over American textile hostility and Hawaii suspicion, warning U.S. fleet/base buildups harden Japan's resolve to fight.
subfiles.title: Intelligence Report: Interview with Japanese Consul General Teijiro Tamura

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 1935 on court-martial sentences and Hirota Cabinet policies.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reviews Despatch 1935: insurgents were condemned for indiscipline, not assassination; summarizes Hirota's defense-expansion, tax, power-nationalization, synthetic fuel, education, and agrarian policies, plus zaibatsu reorganization for defense.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1935 regarding Aftermath of the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch examining the court-martial verdicts for the February 26 rebels and the reform platform of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the verdicts rendered by the special Tokyo Court Martial on the February 26 insurgents, including seventeen death penalties and numerous prison sentences. He observes that punishing military personnel with death for patriotic assassination established a major legal precedent, framed under charges of violating military discipline and unauthorized deployment of troops. The despatch surveys press approval and examines the Hirota Cabinet's subsequent policy platform regarding national defense, administrative reform, and financial reorganization, continuing beyond page 230.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1935: Aftermath of the February 26 Incident
